newsitem.title: BELGIUM: UCB SEES JAPAN ZYRTEC LAUNCH EARLY 1998.
newsitem.headline: UCB SEES JAPAN ZYRTEC LAUNCH EARLY 1998.

text.p: Belgian drugs, fine chemicals and plastic films group UCB said on Wednesday it expected to launch its star anti-allergy drug Zyrtec on the Japanese market early in 1998.

Chief executive officer Georges Jacobs told a results news conference he could not give a precise date for the start of sales in Japan. "We expect to get a registration towards the end of the year and plan to launch early next year."
Asked about a target for Zyrtec sales in Japan, Jacobs said, "I prefer to be very cautious. Japan is a very big market."
UCB would launch Zyrtec in Japan together with Sumitomo and an additional partner. Jacobs gave no details.
In the U.S. where Zyrtec has been on the market for over 20 months, sales by UCB and its partner Pfizer reached $115 million in the first half.

The pharma sector is by far the largest contributor to ordinary profits at UCB. In the first half, pharma profit rose to 2.36 billion francs from 1.93 billion in the same 1996 period. At the group level ordinary profit increased by 33 percent to 3.89 billion francs.
Jacobs said he saw more potential for Zyrtec in the U.S. "It is a huge market of which we only have a small share...16 percent. We hope for another increase in 1998."
He said the market share was much below what UCB had in Europe. "In Europe we are ahead of the competition. In the States we are behind because we started later."
With Zyrtec UCB was market leader in Europe, he said, reiterating the sales target for Zyrtec in the U.S. for this year was "up to" $250 million.
Asked whether UCB was taking measures to limit its dependence on Zyrtec, he said UCB was working on new drugs "around" Zyrtec. "We are confident that we will consolidate the Zyrtec position."

Jacobs said UCB was making good progress on developing an anti-allergy drug, LO 59, which was at the end of clinical trials. It might file for registration in 1998 and was hoping for a launch in the year 2000.
A cardio-vascular drug was moving onto clinical testing on a larger number of patients. "By the end of the year we will know whether we have a drug and should file," he said.
